Mission towns run by the Jesuits among the Guaraní in the Paraná and Uruguay river lands, now parts of Paraguay, Argentina and Brazil, from 1609 to 1767.

At their height about thirty towns held over 100,000 people. Each had a large church, a central plaza, workshops, fields and herds. The Guaraní kept their language, which the Jesuits wrote down and printed. The towns became famous for their music, carving and building.

The missions were also a refuge. Slave raiders from São Paulo in Portuguese Brazil hunted them. The Spanish crown let the Guaraní carry guns, and in 1641 a mission army defeated the raiders at Mbororé.

In 1750 a treaty gave seven missions to Portugal, and the Guaraní who refused to leave were crushed in war. In 1767 the Spanish king expelled the Jesuits from all of Spanish America, and the towns soon emptied. The ruins of San Ignacio Miní and Trinidad are World Heritage Sites.
sum: Mission towns run by the Jesuits among the Guaraní in the Paraná and Uruguay river lands, now parts of Paraguay, Argentina and Brazil, from 1609 to 1767.
